During Ramchandra Ray’s escape, Udayaditya takes charge: Sitaram reluctantly admits he must enforce the order keeping everyone inside, but refuses to fight the prince and offers his weapon, allowing Udayaditya to disarm and bind him before leaving. On the night of Udayaditya’s escape, the roles reverse: Sitaram comes to the prison, gets Udayaditya out under cover of the fire, and leads him away.

Pratapaditya first orders two Pathan men to kill Basanta Ray when he stops at the Simultali inn on his way to Jessore, but the attempt fails when one Pathan cannot bring himself to kill him. Later, Muktiyar Khan carries out Pratapaditya’s written death order, and Abdul kills Basanta Ray with a sword.

In the inner quarters, Ramai is disguised as a middle-aged woman when Rammohan lifts and carries him off. Later, in the king’s room, Ramai appears as himself, the jester, and Rammohan grabs him by the neck and throws him out.
Mangala (Rukmini) secretly prepared poison, which Surma took, believing her time had come. This—not the decree—caused her departure.

Her refusal is taken as a grave insult by Ramchandra Ray, who retaliates by marrying another woman. When Vibha later returns, she finds that she has lost her place in her husband’s home and her hopes of happiness are shattered.

Rukmini takes Udayaditya’s signet ring after he gives it to her, and its seal bears his name. Sitaram and Bhagavat use it to stamp a forged petition that appears to show Udayaditya accusing Pratapaditya of treason and appealing to the Emperor for the kingdom. Bhagavat presents the petition to Pratapaditya as though it had been carried by one of Udayaditya’s servants, and Pratapaditya uses it as a pretext to imprison Udayaditya, despite doubting its authenticity.

Ramchandra’s escape left Sitaram and Bhagavat dismissed and without support. Udayaditya gave them stipends, and when Pratapaditya forbade further aid, Surma secretly arranged payments to their families. A trusted maid let Mangala learn of the payments, and word reached Pratapaditya. Enraged by Surma’s defiance, he ordered her sent to her paternal home.

The song expresses Basanta Ray’s profound loneliness and grief at being left without the loved ones who once filled his life with joy. He sings it first alone at sunset in Raigarh, reflecting on their absence; later, he sings it while taking Vibha’s hand in the silent, empty palace at Jessore, where their absence is made painfully immediate.

Rukmini tried to warn the palace guards about Udayaditya’s escape, but they ignored her, allowing him to flee with Basanta Ray. She later exposed the escape and helped Pratapaditya’s men locate Udayaditya in Raigarh. Pratapaditya then ordered Basanta Ray’s death. When Muktiyar Khan’s soldiers captured Udayaditya, they carried out that order and killed Basanta Ray.

Pratapaditya receives Ramchandra coolly and without ceremony, treating him almost as an afterthought while attending to state business. Ramchandra later reverses the slight in his own court, where he and his courtiers mock Pratapaditya as inferior and boast that Ramchandra outranks him.

Rukmini, the widow Udayaditya had once confessed to being tempted by in Raigarh, returns under the assumed name Mangala and settles near Jessore. She insinuates herself into the palace through its servants and the Rajmahishi, preparing poison intended to kill Surma. After Surma dies, Rukmini enters Udayaditya’s room during a storm, plays on his guilt by claiming he ruined her, and demands his love. Her return deepens his grief and helps bring tragedy into his life.

His early lament begins with Udayaditya wishing he had never been born the crown prince: he feels his royal birth has subjected him to constant scrutiny, neglect, and expectations he cannot meet. He admits he lacks the ability to rule, and later says he would leave everything and go away with Surma. After being brought back as a prisoner, he turns that lifelong sense of unfitness into a formal renunciation: he tells Pratapaditya he does not want the kingdom, swears before Ma-Kali never to claim any part of Jessore or sit on its throne, and names Samaraditya as the heir. He asks only to be released and allowed to leave for Kashi.

When Rammohan refused to carry Ramchandra Ray’s letter to Jessore, Ray gave it to Nayanchand instead. Afraid of what Pratapaditya might do if he saw it, Nayanchand handed it to the Mahishi, who kept it from both Pratapaditya and Vibha. The letter said that Ray had renounced Vibha and that she should not be sent to Chandradwip. Basanta Ray read it and mistook it for a message written in anger, believing Ray would welcome Vibha once she returned. He advised the Mahishi to tell Vibha that her husband had requested her return, so Vibha was led to believe he had understood and forgiven her.

Pratapaditya orders the canal beside the palace blocked with large sal-wood logs, hoping to stop Ramchandra’s boat. But Rammohan and his men haul the boat up and over the logs, so it gets through and escapes.

Basanta Ray’s sitar is his cherished companion and a source of joy, but as Udayaditya’s troubles deepen, grief makes it impossible for him to play: his tears blur his eyes and choke his voice. When he leaves, he abandons the sitar, saying he will never play it again. Later, without Udayaditya, he says its strings are broken and it can no longer be tuned—a reflection of his own broken spirit and lost capacity for joy.

Earlier, Udayaditya was known for boldly resisting oppression and protecting his subjects, even when it meant defying his father. After Surma’s death, fear of Pratapaditya overwhelmed him: he fled rather than stop an official beating a subject, abandoned plans to prevent a planned raid and arson, and no longer dared to help needy subjects financially.
Sitaram helps Udayaditya escape the imprisonment caused by the forged petition: he sets a fire as a diversion, opens the prison door, and leads Udayaditya out to safety.

On the first occasion, Rammohan tied thick sheets into a rope, secured it to a pillar on the palace roof, and carried King Ramchandra Ray on his back down toward the boat. He then carefully lowered the king into it and climbed down himself.

On the second, after Vibha was rejected and fainted in the palace, Rammohan lifted her and carried her out. He placed her in a palanquin near the gate, then returned to the boat.

In Jessore, Vibha is dressed by her mother in elaborate royal finery: thick gold bangles, diamond bracelets, a large nose ring, and carefully restyled hair. Though uncomfortable with the adornments, she is joyful and shyly radiant as she prepares to welcome Ramchandra. In Chandradwip, she rejects royal treatment and goes to him dressed as a common woman, refusing a palanquin and saying she will go like a beggar. Her veil falls as she enters the palace like an ordinary maidservant, unwelcomed, and she falls at Ramchandra’s feet.

After Surma’s death, the window is a place of absence and longing: Udayaditya sits where she used to sit, hoping against hope that she will appear there again. In prison, the small window becomes a symbol of freedom and hope. The glimpse of sky and flying birds lets him imagine that his own “cage” may one day break; to him, the window’s patch of sky is freedom, while the comfortable bed away from it feels like another prison.

At first, Sitaram uses playful flirtation to borrow money from Rukmini, promising to repay it while she indulges him and pretends not to care about interest. He calls her affectionate names, jokes his way out of discussing the debt, and continues visiting her as the money remains unpaid. Their relationship later turns openly hostile: when Udayaditya is imprisoned, Sitaram blames and threatens Rukmini, while she insists the Yubaraj is hers to help or harm.

After helping arrange Udayaditya’s escape, Sitaram returns to Rukmini’s cottage intending to take her money, believing she is dead. Finding her alive, he tries to revive their old playful intimacy, but she is consumed by rage and vows to kill him and Udayaditya. She goes to fetch a curved blade, and Sitaram escapes just before she can attack him.

Sitaram first uses the guardhouse fire as a distraction: while the guards and palace staff rush to fight the blaze, Udayaditya’s cell is left unguarded, allowing Sitaram to get him out. He then turns the escape into a cover-up. His men deliberately spread and prolong the fire, and Sitaram sets the now-empty prison cell alight, planting bones, a skull, and Udayaditya’s sword inside. He sends people running with false claims that the prince is trapped, screaming, and dead, so the guards believe the cell has collapsed around him. The staged evidence and rumors lead the palace to report Udayaditya’s death in the fire, giving Sitaram time to flee with his family—though Rukmini later exposes the plot.
He dismisses Udayaditya’s rescue as nothing more than an expected duty—believing Udayaditya acted mainly for his sister’s sake—and later joins in mocking him in court, without gratitude.

Pratapaditya first dismisses the Emperor’s anger as an “empty fear,” refusing to be deterred by the threat of Delhi’s soldiers. Later, Bhagavat turns that fear into a trap: he forges a petition bearing Udayaditya’s seal, pretending the prince has accused his father of treason and appealed to the Emperor for the kingdom. Bhagavat delivers it to Pratapaditya as if he had intercepted it on its way to Delhi, making the Emperor’s authority the pretext for treating his son as a traitor and imprisoning him.

At first, Vibha’s hair is a sign of Surma’s living care and closeness: on the day Vibha is dressed for her husband’s visit, she slips away to Surma to have her hair styled as she likes. Later, with Surma gone, the daily ritual becomes an absence made visible. Vibha sits waiting for Surma to braid her hair, but no one comes; evening falls and it remains unbraided. Much later, Rammohan finds her hair unkempt, along with her sorrowful face and dark circles—an outward sign of how alone and neglected she has become in the palace.
